claims.text: In situ high-resolution transmission electron microscopy with a heating stage can reveal atomic-scale thermal behavior changes in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Such an in situ experiment can test whether thermodynamic effects are responsible for enhanced thermal stability.
The as-synthesized AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles are uniform and nearly equiatomic.
The AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles have a single-phase solid-solution structure at room temperature.
Controlled heating can be performed on the nanoparticles inside an in situ HR-TEM setup.
High-vacuum heating conditions will avoid extrinsic oxidation.
A controlled temperature ramp will avoid beam-induced damage.
Increasing temperature activates atomic mobility and accelerates atomic or defect rearrangement.
Heating induces atomic diffusion and local rearrangements within the AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticle lattice.
Thermodynamic contributions may drive local phase segregation or ordering transitions during heating.
Local segregation or ordering processes will be directly visible at atomic scale under in situ HR-TEM heating.
At a threshold temperature, clustering, phase segregation, ordering, or other atomic-level changes will become apparent relative to the room-temperature structure.
The room-temperature baseline has a homogeneous distribution of Au, Co, Cu, Ni, and Pt atoms.
Sintering and beam-induced artifacts can mask intrinsic thermal behavior.
Instrument resolution and beam effects may limit precise determination of transition temperatures and activation energies.
Parallel controls without beam exposure can distinguish thermally induced changes from beam damage.
The proposed thermodynamic interpretation is falsified if no significant rearrangement or transition occurs under heating, or if all observed changes are caused by the electron beam.
